title: Keyboard Concerto No. 1 in D minor
hook: The whole band and the soloist start in stark octaves, and the drive in D minor hardly lets up.

painting.title: Dresden from the Right Bank of the Elbe below the Augustus Bridge
painting.pairingNote: The dome of the Frauenkirche, where Bach played the new Silbermann organ in 1736, rises over the city he visited as Saxon court composer; one theory links these concertos to his visit of 1738.

facts: Around 1738, in Leipzig, Bach wrote out a set of concertos for harpsichord and strings in his own hand. This one stands first. Parts for an earlier version had already been copied in 1734 by his son Carl Philipp Emanuel.

The music is older than the manuscript. In 1726 and 1728 Bach had used all three movements in two church cantatas, with the solo part played on the organ. For a long time scholars believed the concerto began as a lost violin concerto, because the solo part is full of violin figures. In 2016 two Bach scholars, Christoph Wolff and Gregory Butler, argued instead for an organ concerto from Bach’s first years in Leipzig. The question is open.

Why Bach gathered these concertos is not known. One theory links them to the Collegium Musicum, a society of students and musicians that Bach directed and that gave weekly concerts at Zimmermann’s coffee house in Leipzig. Another, Peter Wollny’s, links them to a visit to the court at Dresden in 1738.

After Bach’s death the concerto was kept alive in the circle of Felix Mendelssohn: his sister Fanny played it in Berlin in 1824, and he played it in Leipzig in 1835. Today it is played on the harpsichord or, as here, on the piano.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a stern, driving opening (I), a long song over a repeating bass (II), a whirlwind finale (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: The strings and the piano open together on one bare line in octaves, hard and insistent. That refrain, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], keeps returning, while the piano breaks away in longer and longer solos full of rapid, flickering figures. Late in the movement the piano plays almost alone in a long, brilliant run before the band closes the door.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a stark tune played by everyone in [[unison|unison]], built on repeated notes and jagged leaps.

mainIdeas.name: The flicker
mainIdeas.description: the piano alternates quickly between a moving note and a repeated one, a figure borrowed from violin playing.

stops.happening: The ritornello, in [[unison|unison]], in D minor

stops.hear: The piano breaks away on its own with running notes; the strings answer with short chords
The music lurches between two minor keys, D minor and A minor, without warning
stops.happening: Abrupt shifts that give the opening an old, severe colour

stops.hear: The piano starts a new figure: one note repeated rapidly against moving notes
Now and then the strings break in with the refrain in a major key, a sudden brightness in the dark

stops.hear: The opening refrain in octaves again, in D minor

stops.label: Last minute

notice: Listen for the moments when everyone plays the same line in octaves. They sound like a wall, and they mark the structure of the movement.
In the central section, follow the piano’s repeated notes. On a violin this figure would be played by rocking the bow across two strings.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A slow movement in G minor built over a [[ground-bass|ground bass]]: a line played first by everyone together, in octaves, and then repeated underneath while the piano spins a long, decorated melody above it. The bass moves to other keys and comes home, and the opening line returns to close.

mainIdeas.name: The ground
mainIdeas.description: a slow, solemn line, first heard in [[unison|unison]].

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: the piano’s high, ornamented melody, which never quite repeats itself.

stops.hear: Strings and piano together, slowly, on one heavy line in octaves
stops.happening: The ground bass, stated in unison

stops.hear: The piano enters high up with a winding, decorated melody; the strings keep the slow line going below
stops.happening: The first solo over the ground

stops.hear: The bass line moves to new keys; the piano’s melody grows more elaborate
The bass returns to G minor and the piano’s line starts to settle

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Everyone together on the slow line in octaves
stops.happening: The opening returns to close the movement

notice: Hum the slow line from the opening. Once you know it, you can hear it underneath the piano for the rest of the movement.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A fast finale in three that sets off at full speed and keeps going. As in the first movement, the refrain swings between D minor and A minor, the piano’s solos grow longer and wilder, and near the end the music stops on a held chord, where the soloist may add a short [[cadenza|cadenza]], before the band’s last refrain.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a vigorous tune in quick notes, started by the violins and the piano and taken up at once by the rest.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s figures
mainIdeas.description: bouncing patterns that leap between registers.

stops.hear: The violins and the piano launch a quick, energetic tune; the other strings join a moment later
The music jumps between D minor and A minor

stops.hear: The piano takes over with bouncing, virtuoso figures
The band’s tune returns for a few bars, then the piano launches a long, brilliant solo

notice: Compare the opening of this movement with the opening of the first. Both begin with a bare, driving line and the same jolts between two minor keys.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Murray Perahia plays a modern Steinway and directs the Academy of St Martin in the Fields from the keyboard, as Bach would have directed from the harpsichord. The recording was made at Air Studios in London in May 2000. A theorbo, a large Baroque lute, is listed among the players, adding chords to the bass line.

threads.title: Octaves as a frame
threads.body: The first two movements open with everyone in unison, and the finale starts almost the same way. Each time the bare line marks the start and the end.

threads.title: A violin in disguise
threads.body: Whatever the original instrument was, the solo part is full of figures that come from the violin: repeated notes, rocking between strings, wide leaps.

threads.title: Minor keys throughout
threads.body: D minor, G minor, D minor. The brighter moments are short, which is why they stand out.
